extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and readers concerned with peer-review integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and community-sourced recommendations for detecting, preventing, and responding to manipulation of the scholarly peer-review process (especially author-recommended/fake reviewers). Intended to inform editorial policy and reviewer-selection practices across journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit or eliminate author-recommended reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should not rely on (or should severely limit) reviewers suggested by authors, because that practice has been implicated in peer-review rigging and fake-review scams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use at most one suggested reviewer and give less weight to author suggestions; consider removing the option entirely since publishers implemented this system and it has been abused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify reviewer identity and contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should verify that suggested or recruited reviewers are real and contactable persons (preferably via institutional addresses), to prevent fake reviewers using bogus emails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer legitimate institutional e-mail addresses with the reviewer's name as part of the address; if a private email (gmail/yahoo/etc.) is provided, cross-check via Google Scholar, institutional pages, or other professional profiles before using the reviewer. Note: commenters caution gmail can be legitimate, so verification rather than outright exclusion is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use executive editors or oversight for inexperienced EICs
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should appoint experienced executive editors to oversee and mentor editors-in-chief, helping detect and prevent fraud and poor editorial practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive editors can guide new EICs in reviewer selection, plagiarism checks and other front-end screening tasks; they provide institutional memory and quality control across journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor-initiated reviewer solicitation (don’t rely on authors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should actively search for and solicit referees (e.g., using Google and literature searches) rather than depending on author-provided reviewer lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searching for referees by topic yields real faculty members with subject-matter expertise; takes more time but produces more reliable reviewers than unvetted suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use online searches to detect plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Google or other web-search tools to check manuscript text for plagiarized passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors can search suspicious passages to catch copying; if plagiarism is detected, reject the paper without opportunity for resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare manuscript versions to detect data falsification
rubrics_metrics.description: Check each version of the manuscript and the galleys to ensure numbers and results do not change fraudulently across versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracking changes across versions helps detect data massaging or falsification introduced during revision stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase number of reviewers and reduce reliance on single suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Using more reviewers reduces the influence of any single (possibly fraudulent) reviewer and increases robustness of the evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasing reviewer count and reducing the role of author-suggested reviewers makes the process more democratic and less vulnerable to manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a vetted pool of professional reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain and use a pool of reviewers who are known, vetted, and selected for integrity and expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A curated pool of trustworthy reviewers reduces dependence on ad-hoc or author-suggested reviewers; such lists should be actively maintained and quality-controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name reviewers on accepted papers (increase transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Add reviewers' names to accepted papers to increase transparency and accountability in peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing reviewer names (with consent) can deter fraudulent behavior and promote sharing of review experience; may require policy changes and reviewer agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt double-blind peer review where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use double-blind review (authors and reviewers anonymized) to reduce bias and some conflict-of-interest pathways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-blind review can limit nepotism and bias, though it is not a panacea for identity-based manipulation; combine with other safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable post-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage and permit critical post-publication review to catch problems missed during pre-publication review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-publication platforms (e.g., PubPeer) allow ongoing scrutiny; policies should address harassment/witch-hunt concerns while supporting legitimate critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomize reviewer selection from a qualified pool
rubrics_metrics.description: Select reviewers by randomization from a vetted qualified pool to reduce selection bias and collusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires a clean, well-curated database of qualified reviewers; the page notes existing publisher databases may be corrupted and need rebuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slow down review throughput for quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor fewer publications, longer peer times, and more careful screening rather than rapid acceptance and high output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer, more careful review cycles reduce opportunities for rushed or superficial peer review that can be exploited for fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide financial incentives or formal recognition for reviewers/editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider compensating reviewers and editors (and providing royalties to authors) to improve motivation and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetary or formal rewards could foster responsibility and possibly reduce low-quality reviews, though commenters debate feasibility and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold editors and editorial boards publicly accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: Make editors and editorial board members accountable for the journals they oversee; they should be reachable and subject to scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public responsibility includes transparency about editorial changes; editors who enable poor practices should be exposed or asked to resign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require a named, contactable person to take responsibility (personal accountability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a model like CE certification where a named, identifiable person takes complete personal responsibility for the integrity of published data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal accountability may deter sloppy or fraudulent practices; commenters suggested this model has worked in safety-critical certification systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure publisher submission systems against exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that vulnerabilities in publishers' computerized submission systems can be exploited to create fake reviewer identities; secure those systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical fixes and better authentication processes are needed to prevent identity theft and automated fraud in editorial platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject plagiarism outright
rubrics_metrics.description: If plagiarism is found during screening, reject the manuscript without opportunity for resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should routinely check for plagiarism and act decisively to maintain integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflicts of interest in reviewer selection (no collaborators/ex-students)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not select collaborators, ex-students, or close friends as reviewers because they may not provide impartial assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters note this practice is common and problematic; editors should screen for prior relationships and potential conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archive evidence and use community scrutiny for suspected cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When investigating suspicious publications, archive screenshots and PDFs, contact editorial board members, and report findings on community platforms (e.g., PubPeer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps for whistleblowers/sleuths include downloading PDFs, taking screenshots for archival purposes, contacting editors, and posting on public forums to gather scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase transparency in retraction notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish more informative retraction notices that explain the background and reasons, instead of vague lawyer-drafted statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater transparency about retractions helps the community understand systemic failures and hold responsible parties accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about relying solely on publisher databases / keywords
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher reviewer-databases built on keywords and self-declared specializations can be corrupted and manipulated; they should be rebuilt and validated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not trust database affiliations/keywords blindly; active curation and validation are necessary to maintain a trustworthy reviewer pool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider collective actions (boycotts/embargoes) to pressure publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: As a policy lever, institutions or researchers might collectively withhold fees or subscriptions to force publisher reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters propose embargoes or boycotts as extreme measures to pressure large publishers; this is a strategic/political remedy rather than a technical editorial safeguard.
